grammar.title: SIMPLE, CONTINUOUS OR PERFECT
points: Present perfect (have/has + past participle): past events with no finished time given, often with just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for. 'I've already seen that film.'
Past simple: finished actions at a stated past time. 'We moved here in 2019.'
Past perfect (had + past participle): something that happened before another past moment. 'When I arrived, the bus had left.'
Present continuous: actions happening now, temporary situations, and annoying habits with always. 'He's always interrupting me.'
Past continuous: background actions or actions in progress at a past moment. 'It was raining when we went out.'
questions: I ____ (never / try) sushi before, so I'm a bit nervous. | have never tried
We ____ (move) to Valencia in 2019. | moved
When we got to the cinema, the film ____ (already / start). | had already started
Be quiet! The baby ____ (sleep). | is sleeping
My sister ____ (always / take) my charger without asking. It's so annoying! | is always taking
While I ____ (wait) for the bus, it started to snow. | was waiting
Correct it: I have seen Marta yesterday. | I saw Marta yesterday.
She ____ her homework yet. (hasn't finished / didn't finish) | hasn't finished
It was the first time he ____ (fly) in a helicopter. | had flown
This is the second time I ____ (lose) my keys this week. | have lost
They ____ here since 2020. (live / have lived / lived) | have lived
Correct it: What do you do right now? | What are you doing right now?

grammar.title: PRESENT PERFECT SIMPLE AND CONTINUOUS
points: Both tenses link the past to now, without saying exactly when something happened.
Present perfect simple: a finished action with a result now, or how many / how often. 'I've written two emails.'
Present perfect continuous (have/has been + -ing): focus on the activity or how long, maybe unfinished. 'I've been writing emails all morning.'
It also explains visible results of a recent activity: 'You're dirty! Have you been playing football?'
State verbs (know, have = own, like, believe) don't take the continuous: 'I've known her for years.'
With live, work, study and similar verbs, both forms are possible with little change in meaning.
questions: I ____ (read) three chapters so far today. | have read
Your eyes are red. ____ (you / cry)? | Have you been crying

grammar.title: THE GRAMMAR OF PHRASAL VERBS
points: A phrasal verb is a verb + one or two particles (adverb or preposition). The meaning is often not literal: 'give up' = stop trying.
Some have no object: 'The plane took off late.'
Verb + adverb + object: a noun object can go before or after the particle ('turn off the TV' / 'turn the TV off'), but a pronoun must go in the middle: 'turn it off'.
Verb + preposition + object: the object always comes after the preposition, even a pronoun: 'I'll look after him.'
Three-part verbs (verb + adverb + preposition) keep the object at the end: 'I get on with them.'
questions: Replace the noun with a pronoun: Turn off the radio. | Turn it off.
Correct it: I'll look the children after. | I'll look after the children.
That music is too loud. Please ____. (turn down it / turn it down) | turn it down

Correct it: She gets on her cousins with. | She gets on with her cousins.

grammar.title: MODALS (1): NECESSITY, OBLIGATION, PROHIBITION AND ADVICE
points: need to = it is necessary; don't need to / needn't = it isn't necessary. 'You need to book early.'
must: the speaker feels it is obligatory. have to: the rule comes from outside. 'I must call Gran.' 'We have to wear a uniform.'
mustn't = it is forbidden. don't have to = it's optional. They are very different! 'You mustn't run here.' 'You don't have to come.'
should / ought to give advice; shouldn't says something is a bad idea. 'You ought to rest.'
must has no past form: use had to. 'Yesterday I had to stay late.'
questions: You ____ touch that wire. It's dangerous! (mustn't / don't have to) | mustn't
Tomorrow is a holiday, so we ____ get up early. (mustn't / don't have to) | don't have to

Correct it: You ought see a doctor. | You ought to see a doctor.
In my school, students ____ wear a uniform. It's a rule. (have to / should) | have to
Correct it: She musts finish it today. | She must finish it today.
Past of must: Yesterday I ____ stay late at school. | had to
You ____ bring food. There's plenty here. (needn't / mustn't) | needn't
Correct it: He don't have to come. | He doesn't have to come.

Complete with one word: You ought ____ apologise to her. | to

grammar.title: PRESENT AND PAST HABITS
points: Present habits: present simple + frequency adverb (before the main verb, after be) or a frequency phrase at the end. 'I hardly ever eat meat.' 'We meet from time to time.'
always / constantly / continually + present continuous shows a habit annoys you: 'She's always borrowing my pens.'
used to + infinitive: past habits and states that are no longer true. Negative and question: didn't use to / Did you use to ...?
would + infinitive: repeated past actions only, never states. 'Every Sunday we would visit Gran.' (NOT 'I would have a dog.')
always / constantly + past continuous: annoying habits in the past. 'He was always forgetting his book.'
questions: When I was little, I ____ be afraid of dogs. (used to / use to) | used to
Correct it: I didn't used to like olives. | I didn't use to like olives.

Put the adverb in the right place: I eat meat. (rarely) | I rarely eat meat.

grammar.title: BE/GET USED TO
points: be used to + noun or -ing: something is normal for you now. 'I'm used to the noise.'
get used to + noun or -ing: something is slowly becoming normal. 'I'm getting used to my new school.'
Here 'to' is a preposition, so the next verb takes -ing: 'She's used to cooking for ten people.' (NOT 'used to cook')
be and get can go in any tense: 'I wasn't used to it', 'You'll get used to it', 'He has got used to it'.
Don't confuse it with used to + infinitive, which is a past habit: 'I used to cycle to school.'
questions: I'm used to ____ (get) up early, so 6 a.m. is no problem. | getting

grammar.title: NARRATIVE TENSES
points: Past simple tells the main events of a story in order: 'She opened the box and smiled.'
Past continuous sets the scene or shows an action in progress: 'The wind was blowing hard.'
Past perfect simple (had + past participle): a completed action before another past event. 'By the time we arrived, they had eaten.'
Past perfect continuous (had been + -ing): an activity that went on for some time before a past moment. 'I had been waiting for an hour when he came.'
State verbs (know, be, have = own) are not used in the continuous: 'I had known him for years.'

grammar.title: FUTURE (1): REVIEW
points: Present simple for timetables and fixed schedules: 'My flight leaves at noon.' Present continuous for arrangements with other people: 'I'm seeing the dentist on Friday.'
be going to: intentions already decided, and predictions from what you can see now. 'It's going to fall!'
will: decisions made at the moment of speaking, offers, promises and predictions based on opinion. 'I'll carry that for you.'
be about to + verb: something will happen in the next few moments. 'The match is about to start.'
After when, until, before, after, as soon as, use a present tense (or present perfect), not will: 'I'll phone when I arrive.'
questions: The train ____ (leave) at 6.45 tomorrow morning. | leaves

grammar.title: FUTURE (2): CONTINUOUS AND PERFECT
points: Future continuous (will be + -ing): an action in progress at a future moment. 'At ten tomorrow I'll be sitting my exam.'
It is also a polite way to ask about plans: 'Will you be using the computer later?'
Future perfect (will have + past participle): an action finished before a future moment, often with by. 'By Friday I'll have read the book.'
Future perfect continuous (will have been + -ing): how long something will have lasted at a future point. 'In May we'll have been living here for a year.'
State verbs take the simple perfect form: 'Next year they'll have been married for ten years.'
questions: This time next week, I ____ (lie) on a beach. | will be lying

grammar.title: MODALS (2): MODALS IN THE PAST
points: would have + past participle: something imagined in the past that didn't really happen. 'You would have laughed!'
should have / ought to have + past participle: criticism or regret about the past. 'I should have listened.' shouldn't have = it was a mistake to do it.
needn't have + past participle: you did something, but it turned out to be unnecessary. 'You needn't have cooked; we'd already eaten.'
didn't need to + infinitive: it wasn't necessary, so you probably didn't do it. 'I didn't need to queue because I had a ticket.'
All of these use have + past participle, never a past simple form: 'should have gone' (NOT 'should have went').

grammar.title: RELATIVE CLAUSES
points: Defining clauses say which person or thing we mean. No commas. Use who/that for people, which/that for things: 'The boy who sits next to me is Dutch.'
You can leave out who/which/that when it is the object of the clause: 'The film (that) we watched was long.' You can't when it is the subject.
Non-defining clauses add extra information between commas. Never use that and never leave the pronoun out: 'My aunt, who lives in Vigo, is a vet.'
whose = possession, where = places, when = times: 'a friend whose mum is a chef', 'the day when we met'.
which can refer to a whole idea: 'He arrived late, which annoyed everyone.'
Prepositions usually go at the end ('the girl I spoke to'); in formal style they go before whom/which ('the girl to whom I spoke').
questions: That's the girl ____ brother plays for Betis. (who / whose / which) | whose
This is the town ____ I was born. (which / where / that) | where
My mum, ____ is a nurse, works nights. (who / that) | who

Can the pronoun be left out? 'The book that I bought is great.' (yes / no) | yes
Can the pronoun be left out? 'The man who lives next door is a chef.' (yes / no) | no
Madrid, ____ is the capital of Spain, is very hot in summer. (which / that) | which
The boy ____ won the race is my cousin. (who / which / whose) | who
2015 was the year ____ we moved house. (when / where / whose) | when

Formal style: The person to ____ I spoke was helpful. (who / whom / which) | whom
He passed all his exams, ____ surprised everyone. (which / that / what) | which

grammar.title: THE PASSIVE (1): REVIEW
points: Form the passive with be in the right tense + past participle: 'The bridge was built in 1990.' 'Dinner is being cooked.'
Use it when the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant, or when you want to focus on the thing affected: 'My bike has been stolen.'
Add the doer with by only when it matters: 'The song was written by a teenager.'
Verbs with two objects can make the person the subject: 'She was given a prize.'
have / get + object + past participle means someone else does a job for you: 'I had my phone repaired.' Get is more informal.
questions: This castle ____ (build) in the twelfth century. | was built
Be careful! The floor ____ (clean) right now. | is being cleaned

grammar.title: THE PASSIVE (2): OTHER STRUCTURES
points: Passive infinitive = (to) be + past participle. It follows verbs like want, hope, expect, seem: 'Everyone wants to be liked.'
Verb + object + passive infinitive: 'We expect the work to be finished soon.'
After modal verbs there is no to: 'Phones must be switched off.'
-ing passive = being + past participle, after verbs like enjoy, avoid, hate, remember, don't mind: 'I hate being told what to do.'
Use being + past participle after prepositions too: 'She's afraid of being laughed at.'

grammar.title: REPORTED SPEECH
points: When the reporting verb is in the past, the tense usually moves one step back: 'I'm tired' -> She said she was tired. will -> would, can -> could, past simple / present perfect -> past perfect.
No change is needed when the reporting verb is in the present ('He says he likes it'), or when the fact is still true or still in the future.
Pronouns, places and times change: I -> he/she, here -> there, tomorrow -> the next day, yesterday -> the day before.
Reported questions use statement word order and no do/did: 'Where do you live?' -> He asked where I lived. Yes/no questions use if or whether.
Orders and requests: tell / ask + person + (not) to + verb: 'She told me to wait.' Remember: say something, but tell someone something.
questions: 'I'm hungry.' -> He said he ____ hungry. | was
'I'll help you.' -> She said she ____ help me. | would
'I can swim.' -> He said he ____ swim. | could

'Where do you live?' -> She asked me where I ____. | lived
He asked me where ____. (was the station / the station was) | the station was

'Don't touch it!' -> She told me ____ it. | not to touch
'I like this song.' -> She says she ____ this song. (likes / liked) | likes

She ____ me that she was leaving. (said / told) | told

grammar.title: MODALS (3): DEDUCTION
points: must + verb: you feel sure something is true. 'They look identical. They must be twins.'
can't / couldn't + verb: you feel sure something is NOT true. (Don't use mustn't for this.) 'That can't be right.'
may / might / could + verb: it is possible. may not / might not = perhaps not. 'She might be at the gym.'
For the past, add have + past participle: 'He must have forgotten.' 'They can't have left yet.' 'I might have lost it.'
For actions in progress use modal + be + -ing: 'He must be joking.'
questions: He's been running for hours. He ____ be exhausted. (must / can't) | must
That ____ be Ana. She's in Paris this week. (must / can't) | can't

Complete with one word: They might not ____ received my email. | have

grammar.title: CONDITIONALS (1): REVIEW
points: Zero conditional: if / when + present, present. For things that are always true. 'If you press this, the screen turns on.'
First conditional: if + present, will / can / might + verb. A real future possibility. 'If I see her, I'll tell her.' unless = if ... not.
Second conditional: if + past simple, would / could / might + verb. Imaginary or unlikely present or future. 'If I were you, I'd apologise.'
Third conditional: if + past perfect, would have + past participle. Imaginary past, often regrets. 'If we had run, we would have caught the bus.'
The if-clause can come first (with a comma) or second (no comma). Don't put will or would in the if-clause.
questions: If you heat ice, it ____ (melt). | melts
If it rains tomorrow, we ____ (stay) at home. | will stay
If I ____ (be) you, I'd tell the truth. | were

grammar.title: CONDITIONALS (2): MIXED
points: Mixed conditionals join two different times in one sentence.
Past condition -> present result: if + past perfect, would / could / might + verb. 'If I had slept more, I wouldn't be tired now.'
Present or general condition -> past result: if + past simple, would have + past participle. 'If I spoke French, I would have understood the film.'
Compare with the pure third conditional, where both parts are in the past: 'If I had slept more, I wouldn't have been tired yesterday.'
Words like now and today show a present result; yesterday or last week show a past result.
questions: If I had eaten breakfast, I ____ (not / be) hungry now. | wouldn't be
If she weren't so lazy, she ____ (finish) the project last week. | would have finished

grammar.title: USES OF VERB + -ING
points: Some verbs are followed by -ing, not the infinitive: enjoy, avoid, deny, admit, consider, suggest, finish, mind, keep, imagine, risk. 'She keeps texting me.'
After a preposition the verb is always -ing: 'good at drawing', 'without asking', 'after leaving school'.
Set expressions take -ing: it's not worth, there's no point, can't help, have difficulty, spend time, be fed up with. 'There's no point complaining.'
The -ing form can be the subject of a sentence: 'Skating is harder than it looks.'
Participle clauses: when both parts have the same subject, an -ing clause can show time or reason. 'Feeling tired, I went to bed.' Negative: 'Not wanting to argue, he left.'

grammar.title: SUBJECT–VERB AGREEMENT
points: Some nouns end in -s but are singular: news, maths, physics, politics, athletics, gymnastics, the United States. 'Politics is complicated.'
everyone, someone, anybody, nobody, etc. take a singular verb, but we refer back with they / their: 'Someone has left their bag.'
When a clause or an -ing phrase is the subject, the verb is singular: 'Making new friends takes time.'
both of, all of, most of, a number of, a couple of + plural noun take a plural verb: 'Both of my cousins live here.'
one of + plural noun takes a singular verb: 'One of the windows is broken.'
With a lot of, the verb agrees with the noun that follows: 'A lot of time is wasted.' 'A lot of people are waiting.'
questions: The news ____ really bad today. (is / are) | is

grammar.title: DETERMINERS
points: the: for something unique, something specific we both know about, or something already mentioned. 'I bought a cake. The cake was delicious.'
a / an: with a singular countable noun when it is one of many or mentioned for the first time. 'She's got a new bike.'
No article: plural and uncountable nouns when we speak in general. 'Dogs need exercise.' 'Sugar is bad for your teeth.'
some, any, plenty of, a lot of, lots of go with both plural countable and uncountable nouns.
(not) much, (a) little, a bit of + uncountable nouns; (not) many, (a) few, several + plural countable nouns.
few / little = not enough (negative idea); a few / a little = some (positive idea). 'I have a few ideas.' 'There is little hope.'
